question.text: How can two people who have never met agree on a shared secret key when an eavesdropper reads every message they exchange?
question.known_at: Title (line 1), made concrete in The problem (line 9)
question.result_stated: Yes, in words at the very start: "They never send the key. Each person keeps a private number and sends a public number computed from it... An eavesdropper sees only the public numbers, and no known fast method gets the private numbers back from them."

reply.motive: Reason to care: "A version of it starts most HTTPS connections" (line 5) and "Encryption needs a key that both of them know. They have never met, so every message goes over a public channel" (line 9). Reason for the approach: the failed first idea (line 14: "If Eve cannot get 6 back from 8, Bob cannot either. So each side needs its own private number") and the section 'Why powers, and why mod' ("Each choice blocks a simpler way for Eve to find a private number").
reply.close: Yes. Answer (line 75): "The two strangers never send the key. Each sends g raised to a private number, mod p. Each raises the other's public number to their own private number, and both get g^(ab) mod p. Eve sees only g^a and g^b mod p. To get further, Eve must find a or b, and no fast method is known for a large p."
reply.recap: Each side mixes a public base with its own secret exponent mod a prime and swaps the results. Raising the other side's result to your own secret gives you both the same number, and an eavesdropper can only get it by solving the discrete logarithm, which nobody knows how to do fast.
reply.strongest: 'Why powers, and why mod' (lines 43-52): each alternative (no mod, multiplication) is shown failing with concrete numbers, and then the scrambled list of 5^x mod 23 makes 'one-way' visible.
reply.weakest: Line 58: the claim 'about 2048 squarings plus at most 2048 multiplications' rests on a single small example (exponent 6) and never says how a general exponent splits into squarings and multiplications.
suggestions: In line 58, add one sentence: write the exponent in binary; square for each digit, and also multiply by g when the digit is 1.
Briefly say why p is prime (so that every nonzero remainder has an undoing multiplier, and powers of a good g run through all of them).
Name the faster methods in line 56 (for example, the number field sieve), or say plainly that they are beyond scope.
